claims.text: The hierarchical heterostructure can be produced by arc melting followed by homogenization treatments.
The heterostructure contains multiscale grain and precipitate features.
High-resolution imaging can capture the spatial distribution of the hierarchical features.
Imaging can provide quantitative descriptors such as grain-boundary density and secondary-phase distribution.
The proposed model will use microstructural descriptors together with machine learning trained on in-situ tensile and fracture tests.
The quantified hierarchical heterostructure mediates the relationship between processing and mechanical performance.
Correlating microstructural features with measured mechanical responses through machine learning can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior.
The data-driven framework bypasses computationally intensive full-scale simulations.
By bypassing full-scale simulations, the framework will accelerate prediction while maintaining or improving predictive accuracy.
The proposed framework will reduce predictive error by an estimated 10–20% relative to conventional simulation methods.
The proposed framework will reduce computation time by at least a factor of five relative to conventional simulation methods.
The proposed framework will enable faster design iterations and more reliable performance forecasts.
The established finite-element and molecular-dynamics baselines use homogenization assumptions and do not explicitly integrate real-time microstructural data.
The approach may fail if imaging does not adequately capture or quantify the hierarchical features.
The approach may fail if the machine-learning model does not generalize across processing variability.
The approach may fail if unmodeled mechanisms such as complex dislocation dynamics or environmental degradation dominate mechanical behavior.
Independent comparisons will use identical tensile and fracture experiments across multiple HfNbTiVAl10 batches for both the proposed framework and established simulations.
Failure to obtain at least a 10% accuracy improvement and a fivefold computation-time reduction across multiple batches will falsify the hypothesis.
